topic: Non-exam course: Literature post-1900 (Close Reading and Comparative Essay)
subject: english-literature

moments.title: Practical Criticism
moments.body: 1929: I.A. Richards publishes Practical Criticism — an experiment in which he gave undergraduates unsigned poems and analysed their responses. The book argues for close attention to the text itself rather than biographical or historical context. The foundation of close reading.
moments.takeaway: Richards (with Charles Ogden) had also written The Meaning of Meaning (1923). His work is foundational to 20th-century English literary studies.

moments.title: Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity
moments.body: 1930: William Empson, an undergraduate at Cambridge, publishes Seven Types of Ambiguity. Close reading of poetic ambiguity — multiple meanings simultaneously held — as the source of poetic power. The book remains a classic.
moments.takeaway: Empson's argument: ambiguity is not a defect but a strength of poetry. The book is the foundation of modern poetic interpretation.

moments.title: New Criticism in America
moments.who: John Crowe Ransom, Cleanth Brooks, Robert Penn Warren
moments.body: American New Criticism — Ransom's 'The New Criticism' (1941), Brooks's 'The Well Wrought Urn' (1947), Brooks and Warren's textbook 'Understanding Poetry' (1938) — dominates US English departments for two decades. Close reading of the text without biographical or historical context.
moments.takeaway: Wimsatt and Beardsley's 'Intentional Fallacy' (1946) and 'Affective Fallacy' (1949) reject appeal to authorial intent or reader emotion.

now.title: After New Criticism
now.body: New Criticism dominated until structuralism (1960s), poststructuralism (1970s), New Historicism (1980s), and contemporary cultural studies displaced it. But close reading remains the foundation of literary study — even theoretical movements that reject formalism still practice close attention to texts.
now.open_questions: Can close reading be separated from historical context? Recent critics (Franco Moretti, distant reading) propose computational alternatives. The debate continues.

reflection: A set of Cambridge and American mid-20th-century critics taught generations how to read poetry. Whether or not we still accept the New Critical theory, the practice of close reading remains central to the discipline they shaped.
